## 

In our Seaside Chat, we will be teaching about the use of some of the useful functions in tidyverse to work with data, such as:

-   Working with pre-existing data sets

-   Selecting ranges of data that we're interested in exploring

-   Practice with data manipulation

*This activity assumes students are somewhat familiar with the tidyverse package*

# Learning Outcomes

By the end of our Seaside Chat, students will be able to:

-   Use tidyverse functions mutate(), case_when() to successfully create new columns in your dataframe

## Why did we pick this topic?

As you learn new methods for working with data in R, it is important to practice those skills. For more experienced users, it is just as important to continue learning new skills that may improve your effectiveness and efficiency.

We will be working with a pre-existing dataset about crabs. You will need to load the package and the data into R.

Let's get into it!

## 1. Set Up

Load in the required packages and data. Open the data frame and notice the column names. We will have you run some basic functions to check your understanding of the data and structure.

```{r}
#Run this line if you do not have tidyverse already installed
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)

# Load in the package and load in the data
install.packages("HDclassif")
library("HDclassif")

#Load data
data(Crabs)

#Let's explore the data!
#First, let's check the dataframe by clicking on the top-right environment and click on Crabs. You'll see that some of the column names are not very descriptive. Run the followling line to check what the column names represent:

?Crabs

```

You'll see the class column contains two values: the species and the sex. Let's separate them so we can work with both species and sex as individual columns!

## 2. Create new columns using mutate and basic statistical functions

As said before, we want two new columns: species and sex. Enter: mutate!

Before we do that, let's practice a bit more with mutate and what it does.

**What is mutate?** The mutate function is used to both modify existing column in a dataframe or create new ones without messing with any of the other columns. Cool! That means we can do things like add columns together, add an average column, pull out the year from a date, and much more.

Let's start with some basics!

```{r}
# Question: What is the area of a crab's carapace? Create a new column called carapace_area for each individual (row)
Crabs <- Crabs %>% 
  mutate(carapace_area = CL*CW)

```

We can also temporarily mutate columns without permanently committing them to the data frame. *Reminder: By putting Crabs\<- up above, I was creating permanent changes to the data frame. This can be undone by just reloading the data!*

Let's temporarily change the data frame. All of the measurements are in mm. Let's make it into cm!

```{r}
Crabs %>% 
  mutate(CL = CL*10,
         CW = CW*10,
         BD = BD*10,
         FL = FL*10,
         RW = RW*10)
```

Why would you want to do this? You can "pipe in" or %\>% these mutate functions into other things. For example, maybe you want to use ggplot to plot just the frontal lobe size in cm instead of mm. How might you do that?

```{r}
# We started this exercise for you, but you should go ahead and put your ggplot skills to use! Hint: notice for the data mapping in ggplot, when you pipe in and manipulate the data frame, you use a "." where you write data = .
Crabs %>% 
  mutate(FL = FL*10) %>% 
  ggplot(data = ., )
```

Now let's try a cool function! The class column currently lists the species and sex. We will separate it into two separate columns.

**Question: What do you think the str_sub function means? Go ahead and google it and put your answer below. Leave a descriptive comment about what each part of the line is doing.**

```{r}

Crabs <- Crabs %>% 
  mutate(
    Species = str_sub(class, 1, 1),
    Sex = str_sub(class, 2, 2)
  ) 

```

Another way you can achieve the same result:

```{r}
rabs3 <- Crabs %>%
  separate(
    col = class,
    into = c("species", "sex"),
    sep = 1,
    remove = FALSE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    species = case_when(
      species == "B" ~ "Blue",
      species == "O" ~ "Orange",
      TRUE ~ species
    ),
    sex = case_when(
      sex == "M" ~ "Male",
      sex == "F" ~ "Female",
      TRUE ~ sex
    )
  )

```

## 3. Plot

Now, let's see do a quick plot and use Crabs2 to see if there are any differences by species by sex.

```{r}
ggplot(Crabs2, aes(x = CL, fill = sex)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  labs(
    x = "Carapace length (mm) (CL)",
    y = "Count",
    fill = "Sex",
    title = "Crab size (CL) by species and sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

### Question 3.1: What differences can you see?

## 4. Applications

We're interested in using this data to communicate manages of the amount of crabs that are of harvestable length. We're not sure what measurement will be more conservative if CL Carpace length or CW Carpace width. Let's work with CL first.

We'll use the column CL Carapace length (mm) and the case_when() function to create a new column names "CL_harvestable_state" that will take the range of 30-40 mm as "CL_Harvestable", anything under 29.9 mm as "CL_Non-harvestable" and anything over 40.1 mm as "C_Non-harvestable\_ reproductive females_reproductive".

```{r}
# create a new dataframe (Crabs2) with the desired columns
Crabs2 <- Crabs %>%
  mutate(
    CL_harvestable_state = case_when(
      CL >= 30 & CL <= 40 ~ "CL_Harvestable",
      CL <= 29.9 ~ "CL_Non-harvestable",
      CL >= 40.1 ~ "CL_Non-harvestable_reproductive",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
view(Crabs2)
```
